edition: Issue 037: The final poll puts Labour ahead and a party on 5.1 percent named Opportunity in the driver's seat, Bret McKenzie joins the Air Force (sousaphone not required), and a Kiwi turns the New York Marathon into a 14km dance floor
tagline: Your 3-minute Friday reset with one sleep to election day: Labour finally crawls out of the 20s while the keys to the country sit with a party barely over 5 percent, an Oscar winner trades 'Business Time' for service time, and the New York Marathon's most talked-about runner stopped for a 30-second dance at 14km.

stories.headline: Final poll before election puts Labour ahead - and hands the keys to a party on 5.1 percent named Opportunity
stories.summary: With one sleep to voting day, The Post/Freshwater Strategy's last poll has Labour on 30.7% (finally out of the 20s) versus National's 26.4%, with Opportunity at 5.1% in kingmaker position: the National-ACT-NZ First bloc lands on 59 seats, two short of the 61 needed, and polling analysis says Wellington has become an Opportunity stronghold.

body.text: The horse race saved its last plot twist for the morning of the final day. The Post/Freshwater Strategy poll, out this morning, puts Labour on 30.7 percent - up two points since late October and, as RNZ's live coverage put it, finally 'crawling out of the 20s' - with National on 26.4 percent, down 1.2 points in a fortnight. Opportunity, the centrist party led by businesswoman Qiulae Wong, clears the 5 percent threshold on 5.1 percent and is again cast as the kingmaker: on these numbers the National, ACT and NZ First bloc wins a combined 59 seats, two short of the 61 needed to govern. The poll's analysis has Labour's late surge driven by women and under-35s - Hipkins leads by 11.7 points among female voters - while National support has 'suffered a collapse' in Wellington, described as an 'Opportunity stronghold'. It follows Tuesday's final 1News-Verian poll, which had National (29.5%) and Labour (28.8%) neck and neck with Opportunity on 6.2 percent and a projected seven seats, leaving either bloc short of a government without it. Wong says Opportunity will speak first to whichever party wins the most seats. Election night coverage begins 7pm tomorrow, Saturday 7 November.

Two facts to file before your Friday nap. One: whichever bloc wins tomorrow, the next Prime Minister is a Chris - Christopher Luxon or Chris Hipkins - so at minimum the signage and the spell-check stay consistent. Two: the person holding the keys to the country is a party on 5.1 percent that one half of the options has spent the campaign politely declining, making Opportunity the least-likely wedding planner in the democratic world: everyone's keys, one clipboard, and a completely straight face asking whether we'd like the plated dinner or the buffet. We also now have a final poll, a different final poll, and effectively a poll-about-the-polls coming on Monday to adjudicate - the one horse-race everyone agrees on is Saturday. And 'crawling out of the 20s' is a lovely image, but 30.7 percent is less a triumphant exit than a cautious foot through the doorway. Either way: one sleep. Vote like a local who has seen one too many polls.

NZ Herald election live updates (6 Nov 2026, The Post/Freshwater Strategy final pre-election poll): Labour 30.7% (up 2 points since late October), National 26.4% (down 1.2 points in a fortnight), Opportunity 5.1% (down 0.3 on October), Greens 13.0% (down 1.3), NZ First 12.0% (up 0.2), ACT 9.8% (up 0.8), Te Pāti Māori 2.0% (up 0.1). Freshwater Strategy interviewed 1044 eligible voters between 29 October and 3 November; margin of error +/-3%. Seat maths: a combined National-ACT-NZ First bloc would win 59 of the 61 seats needed to govern. The Post's analysis says Labour's momentum is driven by women and under-35s (Hipkins holds an 11.7-point lead among female voters) and that National has 'suffered a collapse' in Wellington, now an 'Opportunity stronghold'. RNZ live (6 Nov 2026): 'Labour crawls out of the 20s in last-minute poll'. Corroboration - final 1News-Verian poll (RNZ/1News, 3 Nov 2026): National 29.5%, Labour 28.8%, Greens 16.4%, ACT 10.0%, NZ First 8.4%, Opportunity 6.2%, Te Pāti Māori 0.4%; 1006 eligible voters polled 29 Oct-2 Nov; Opportunity projected to win seven seats, with both governing blocs short of a majority without it. Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong says the party will speak first to the party with the most seats. Polling day is Saturday 7 November; Stuff/ThreeNews election-night coverage begins 7pm.

stories.headline: Bret McKenzie takes flight with the Air Force: Oscar winner to front the RNZAF band in Wellington
stories.summary: Flight of the Conchords' Bret McKenzie is the featured artist for the RNZAF Band's annual Air Force in Concert at the Michael Fowler Centre on Sunday, with a setlist spanning Muppet soundtracks, the Black Seeds, Conchords classics and solo work - 'What a great way for defence money to be spent,' he says.

body.text: Bret McKenzie has joined the Air Force - the uniform change is optional, the sousaphone is not. The Flight of the Conchords co-founder and Oscar-winning Muppets songwriter is the featured artist for the Royal New Zealand Air Force Band's annual 'Air Force in Concert' performance, this Sunday at Wellington's Michael Fowler Centre. The setlist draws on his entire back catalogue: his time in The Black Seeds, songs he wrote for The Muppets, Flight of the Conchords numbers and solo albums. RNZ reports McKenzie describes the band as 'basically an orchestra... an orchestra without the violins'. The RNZAF Band is a reservist unit drawing players from the wider Wellington music scene, and Band Warrant Officer Ben Robertson says many of them have played with Bret before, making him 'an obvious choice'. Last year's Air Force in Concert featured soul singer Hollie Smith.

We have all, at some point, said the Air Force could really use more Muppets, and finally someone in Defence has listened. 'This is not something you ever just put together. You couldn't hire this many musicians to do a gig for one day,' Bret says of the band - either a lovely tribute to the players or the first defence-procurement sentence a human being has ever understood. And the quote of the week: 'What a great way for defence money to be spent' - the only military-spending endorsement in history to come out of the artist's mouth rather than a White Paper's. Put it in the brochure. A setlist built from the Muppets, the Black Seeds, the Conchords and his solo records is the closest the Air Force has come to a morale strategy you can hum, and the band's most lethal asset remains a man with a sousaphone and perfect timing for the chorus. The most non-combatant of all the armed forces, and frankly we're enlisting.

RNZ (Iain Leggat, 6 Nov 2026, 'Conchord Bret McKenzie takes flight with the Air Force'): McKenzie is the featured artist for the RNZAF Band's annual 'Air Force in Concert' performance on Sunday 8 November at the Michael Fowler Centre, Wellington. The setlist features music from his time with The Black Seeds, songs he wrote for The Muppets, Flight of the Conchords and his solo albums. He told RNZ the band is 'basically an orchestra... an orchestra without the violins', that 'this is not something you ever just put together. You couldn't hire this many musicians to do a gig for one day', and that it is 'a great way for defence money to be spent'. Band Warrant Officer Ben Robertson said the RNZAF Band is a reservist unit made up of players from the wider Wellington music scene and that many have played with McKenzie before, making him 'an obvious choice'. The 2025 Air Force in Concert featured Hollie Smith; in 2025 McKenzie joined the NZSO in Wellington for the family show Creepy-Crawly Carnival.

stories.headline: Kiwi dancer turns the New York Marathon into a dance floor at the 14km mark - and the etiquette police are appalled
stories.summary: Kiwi-born Tongan dancer Elvis Lopeti - whose credits include Lady Gaga's 'Abracadabra' video and Rihanna's Super Bowl halftime show - went viral for a 30-second dance 14km into the New York City Marathon; some online critics called it course obstruction; his response: 'who owns running?'

body.text: Somewhere around the 14km mark of this year's New York City Marathon, running stopped being the point. Kiwi-born Tongan dancer and TikToker Elvis Lopeti went viral after breaking into a dance mid-race, with bystanders capturing the moment. Lopeti is a trained dancer - Lady Gaga's 'Abracadabra' music video, Rihanna's Super Bowl halftime show and the Royal Family Dance Crew are on his CV - and he told RNZ's Checkpoint that race organisers had advised him to have fun, a suggestion he took with professional seriousness: 'Don't tell me to have fun because then I have to put on a bloody show.' He ended up performing three short sets across the 42.2km course, the first lasting about 30 seconds and featuring, in his words, 'some little twerk moves', before tiredness - and darkness - called it. Not everyone was thrilled: some online critics accused him of obstructing the course. Lopeti's defence is disarmingly simple: 'Who owns running?... There's probably an etiquette that I've probably broke... If you're going for a time, just enjoy it because we all ended up walking anyway.'

Rule one of the New York Marathon: do not tell a professional dancer to have fun. That isn't a suggestion, that's a performance contract - the man has danced at a Super Bowl halftime show, so telling him to loosen up at the 14km mark is like handing a fire chief a cupcake and saying 'go wild'. The course-etiquette community has now weighed in, clutching water bottles in horror at the audacity of pausing for 30 seconds in an event where, as Lopeti points out, 'there was most of us walking over a bridge' anyway. Runners cross the line for the medal; he danced for the people who stand cheering for nine hours - and then walked the remaining five, which is both the greatest cardio brag and the most honest review of marathon culture you will read this week. Question for the obstruction committee, though: how is a spontaneous 30-second dance more offensive to the sanctity of the race than the ceremonial mass bridge-walk? Let the man twerk. Boston and London are reportedly next on his list, and somewhere a start-line official is very carefully removing the word 'fun' from next year's athlete guide.

RNZ (6 Nov 2026, 'Most thrilled by Kiwi's "little performance" during NYC marathon - but some called obstruction'): Elvis Lopeti is a Kiwi-born Tongan dancer and TikToker who went viral for dancing about 14km into this year's New York City Marathon. His credits include Lady Gaga's 'Abracadabra' music video, Rihanna's Super Bowl halftime show and the Royal Family Dance Crew. He told RNZ's Checkpoint that race organisers told him to have fun and that he then performed three short dances, the first about 30 seconds ('I was doing some little twerk moves'); after the third he 'got quite tired', it got dark and he walked the rest of the race. Some online commenters criticised him for 'obstructing the course'; his response included 'there's probably an etiquette that I've probably broke... but who owns running?' and 'we all ended up walking anyway'. He called the race a 'once in a lifetime experience' and said he wants to run Boston and London next.
